prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer, $K=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, and $\sigma:K\to K$ be a function with the property that $\sigma(i)=\sigma(j)$ if and only if $i=j$ (in other words, $\sigma$ is a bijection). Show that there is a positive integer $m$ such that $$\underbrace{\sigma(\sigma(\cdots\sigma(i)\cdots))}_{m\text{ times}}=i$$ for all $i\in K$.
answer: Each $i$ returns to itself after some $m_i\le n$ steps; take $m=\operatorname{lcm}(m_1,\dots,m_n)$.

solutions.title: Orbits and the lcm
solutions.body:
Write $\sigma^k$ for $k$-fold composition. Fix $i\in K$. Among $\sigma(i),\sigma^2(i),\dots,\sigma^n(i)$ suppose none equals $i$. Then these $n$ values lie in $K\setminus\{i\}$ ($n-1$ elements), so by pigeonhole $\sigma^a(i)=\sigma^b(i)$ for some $1\le a<b\le n$. Since $\sigma$ is injective we can cancel one $\sigma$ at a time: $\sigma^{a-1}(i)=\sigma^{b-1}(i)$, and so on down to $i=\sigma^{b-a}(i)$, a contradiction with $1\le b-a<n$ and our assumption. Hence $\sigma^{m_i}(i)=i$ for some $1\le m_i\le n$.

Let $m=\operatorname{lcm}(m_1,\dots,m_n)$. Since $\sigma^{m_i}(i)=i$ implies $\sigma^{tm_i}(i)=i$ for all $t\ge1$, we get $\sigma^m(i)=i$ for every $i$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and $P(x)$ an $n$th degree polynomial with real coefficients. (You may cite without proof the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root.)

Show that there is an integer $k\ge\frac n2$ and a sequence of non-constant polynomials with real coefficients $Q_1(x),\dots,Q_k(x)$ such that $P(x)=\prod_{i=1}^kQ_i(x)$.
answer: Peel off a real linear factor, or a real quadratic $(x-\zeta)(x-\bar\zeta)$ for a nonreal root.

solutions.title: Induction on the degree
solutions.body:
We show by strong induction on $n$ that $P$ is a product of non-constant real polynomials each of degree $1$ or $2$; then $k\ge\frac n2$ since the degrees add up to $n$.

For $n=1,2$ take $P$ itself. For $n\ge3$, by the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra $P$ has a complex root $\zeta$.
- If $\zeta$ is real, then $P(x)=(x-\zeta)R(x)$ with $R$ real of degree $n-1$, and we apply the induction hypothesis to $R$.
- If $\zeta$ is nonreal, then $P(\bar\zeta)=\overline{P(\zeta)}=0$ because $P$ has real coefficients, so $\bar\zeta\ne\zeta$ is also a root and $(x-\zeta)(x-\bar\zeta)=x^2-(\zeta+\bar\zeta)x+|\zeta|^2$ has real coefficients and divides $P$ (the quotient has real coefficients, since the division algorithm over $\mathbb R$ gives it). Apply the induction hypothesis to the quotient of degree $n-2$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be an odd positive integer and $P(x)$ a polynomial of degree $n$ with real coefficients. (You may use that $P$ factors as a product of real polynomials each of degree $1$ or $2$, and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.)

Show that $P(x)$ has a real root.
answer: A product of real factors of degree 1 or 2 with odd total degree contains a linear factor.

solutions.title: Parity of the degrees
solutions.body: Write $P=Q_1\cdots Q_k$ with each $Q_i$ real of degree $1$ or $2$ (part (a)). The degrees sum to the odd number $n$, so not all of them are $2$; hence some $Q_j(x)=ax-b$ is linear with $a\ne0$. It has the real root $\frac ba$, which is a root of $P$. ∎

prompt: Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with real coefficients and let $a,b$ be real numbers and $m$ a positive integer. If $\zeta=a+bi$ is a nonreal root of $P(x)$ of multiplicity $m$, show that $\bar\zeta=a-bi$ is also a root of $P(x)$ of multiplicity $m$.
answer: Compare multiplicities of $\zeta$ and $\bar\zeta$ using that $(x-\zeta)^s(x-\bar\zeta)^s$ has real coefficients.

solutions.title: Multiplicity of the conjugate
solutions.body:
Let $s$ be the multiplicity of $\bar\zeta$ (it is at least $1$ since $\bar\zeta$ is a root, as $P(\bar\zeta)=\overline{P(\zeta)}=0$). Write $P(x)=(x-\zeta)^m(x-\bar\zeta)^sR(x)$ with $R(\zeta)\ne0\ne R(\bar\zeta)$.

Suppose $s<m$. Then $P(x)=\big[(x-\zeta)(x-\bar\zeta)\big]^s(x-\zeta)^{m-s}R(x)$, and $(x-\zeta)(x-\bar\zeta)=x^2-2ax+a^2+b^2$ has real coefficients. Dividing $P$ by $[(x-\zeta)(x-\bar\zeta)]^s$ (real coefficients) gives that $S(x)=(x-\zeta)^{m-s}R(x)$ has real coefficients. But $\zeta$ is a root of $S$ (as $m-s\ge1$), so $\bar\zeta$ must also be a root of $S$; however $S(\bar\zeta)=(\bar\zeta-\zeta)^{m-s}R(\bar\zeta)\ne0$, a contradiction.

The case $s>m$ is symmetric (swap the roles of $\zeta$ and $\bar\zeta$). Hence $s=m$. ∎

prompt: Find all positive integers $n\ge3$ such that there exists a permutation $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ of $1,2,\dots,n$ such that $a_1,2a_2,\dots,na_n$ can be rearranged into an arithmetic progression.
answer: No such $n$ exists: for every $n\ge3$ the numbers $a_1,2a_2,\dots,na_n$ can never form an arithmetic progression.

solutions.title: Counting multiples of primes
solutions.body:
Put $t_j=ja_j$ and suppose the $t_j$ form an arithmetic progression (AP) $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with common difference $d$ ($d\ne0$: if all $t_j$ were equal then $a_j=c/j$ and $a_{n-1}=\frac{c}{n-1}$, $a_n=\frac cn$ with $c=a_1\le n$, $n\mid c$ gives $c=n$ and $\frac n{n-1}\notin\mathbb Z$, impossible for $n\ge3$).

**Lemma.** Let $p$ be a prime and $A$ an AP of $k$ integers with difference $d$.
(i) If $p\nmid d$, then the number of terms divisible by $p$ is $\lfloor k/p\rfloor$ or $\lceil k/p\rceil$, and these terms form an AP with difference $pd$.
(ii) If $p\mid d$, all terms are congruent mod $p$, so either none or all are divisible by $p$.
(iii) If $p\nmid d$ and $k_1$ terms are divisible by $p$, then at most $\lceil k_1/p\rceil$ of them are divisible by $p^2$ (apply (i) to the AP of those terms divided by $p$, which has difference $d$).

*Case 1: $n$ prime.* $t_j$ is divisible by $n$ only if $j=n$ or $a_j=n$, so at most $2<n$ terms are, and at least one ($t_n$) is. By (ii) $n\nmid d$, so by (i) exactly $\lceil n/n\rceil=1$ term is divisible by $n$. Hence $j=n$ and $a_j=n$ coincide: $a_n=n$, $t_n=n^2$. This is the largest value any $t_j$ can take, so it is an end term, and the next term is at most $(n-1)^2$ (all other $j,a_j\le n-1$). So $|d|\ge n^2-(n-1)^2=2n-1$ and the other end is $n^2-(n-1)|d|\le n^2-(n-1)(2n-1)=-n^2+3n-1<1$, which is not a valid term ($t_j\ge1$).

*Case 2: $n=9$ or $n\ge12$.* Write $n=3k+m$ ($m\in\{0,1,2\}$, $k\ge3$). Let $c$ be the number of $t_j$ divisible by $3$. These are the $j$ with $3\mid j$ or $3\mid a_j$; both sets have $k$ elements, so $k\le c\le2k<n$. By (ii) $3\nmid d$, so by (i) $c\in\{k,k+1\}$ (and $c=k$ if $m=0$, i.e. $n=9$).
- If $c=k$, then $\{j:3\mid j\}=\{j:3\mid a_j\}$ and for those $j$, $9\mid t_j$: so $k$ terms are divisible by $9$, but by (iii) at most $\lceil k/3\rceil<k$.
- If $c=k+1$, then $|\{3\mid j\}\cap\{3\mid a_j\}|=k-1$ and these $k-1$ terms are divisible by $9$, but by (iii) at most $\lceil\frac{k+1}3\rceil<k-1$ for $k\ge4$ (here $m\ne0$ so $k\ge4$ because $n\ge12$ in this case, or $n=10,11$ which are handled elsewhere).

*Case 3: $n\in\{4,6,8,10\}$.* Parity: let $u$ be the number of $j$ with $j,a_j$ both odd; the number of odd $t_j$ is $u$. If $d$ is odd the parities alternate, so $u=\frac n2$, which forces all odd $j$ to have odd $a_j$ and all even $j$ even $a_j$; then all $\frac n2$ even terms are multiples of $4$. They form an AP with odd difference $2d/2=d$ after halving... precisely halving them gives an AP of $\frac n2$ integers with odd difference, of which at most $\lceil\frac n4\rceil<\frac n2$ are even: contradiction. If $d$ is even all terms have the same parity; all odd is impossible (even $j$ exists), so all even: no $j$ has both $j,a_j$ odd, so $a$ maps odd numbers bijectively onto even numbers and even numbers onto odd numbers. The terms divisible by $4$ are: $j$ odd with $4\mid a_j$ and $j$ even with $4\mid j$ ($a_j$ odd): $2\lfloor n/4\rfloor$ in total. Mod $4$, an AP with $d\equiv2\pmod4$ has exactly $\frac n2$ terms divisible by $4$, and with $4\mid d$ it has $0$ or $n$. For $n=6,10$, $2\lfloor n/4\rfloor=2,4\notin\{\frac n2,0,n\}=\{3,0,6\},\{5,0,10\}$: contradiction. For $n=4,8$ we have $d\equiv2\pmod4$ and $n=2^s$: let $i$ be the index with $a_i=n$; $i$ is odd and $a_n$ is odd (since $a$ swaps parity), so $t_n-t_i=n(a_n-i)$ is a nonzero multiple of $2n$, of $2$-adic valuation $\ge s+1$. If the two terms are $r$ places apart in the AP, $rd=\pm(t_n-t_i)$ gives $v_2(r)+1\ge s+1$, so $2^s=n\le r\le n-1$, a contradiction.

All $n\ge3$ are covered (primes; $4,6,8,10$; $9$ and $n\ge12$), so no such $n$ exists. A computer check of all permutations for $3\le n\le9$ agrees. ∎

prompt:
Fix a positive integer $n$. Pick $4n$ equally spaced points on a circle and color them alternately blue and red. You use $n$ blue chords to pair the $2n$ blue points, and you use $n$ red chords to pair the $2n$ red points. If some blue chord intersects some other red chord, then such a pair of chords is called a "good pair."

For the case $n=3$, explicitly show that there are at least $3$ distinct ways to pair the $2n$ blue points and the $2n$ red points such that there are a total of $3$ good pairs (two configurations of chord pairings are not considered distinct if one of them can be "rotated" to the other).
answer: Three explicit configurations (listed in the solution), each with exactly $3$ blue-red crossings.

solutions.title: Three configurations
solutions.body:
Label the $12$ points $P_0,\dots,P_{11}$ clockwise, with blue points $P_0,P_2,\dots,P_{10}$ and red points $P_1,P_3,\dots,P_{11}$. Chords $P_aP_b$ and $P_cP_d$ ($a<b$, $c<d$) cross exactly when $a<c<b<d$ or $c<a<d<b$.

1. Blue: $P_0P_2,\ P_4P_6,\ P_8P_{10}$. Red: $P_1P_3,\ P_5P_7,\ P_9P_{11}$. The good pairs are $(P_0P_2,P_1P_3)$, $(P_4P_6,P_5P_7)$, $(P_8P_{10},P_9P_{11})$: exactly $3$.
2. Blue: $P_0P_6,\ P_2P_8,\ P_4P_{10}$. Red: $P_1P_3,\ P_5P_7,\ P_9P_{11}$. The red chord $P_1P_3$ crosses only $P_2P_8$, $P_5P_7$ crosses only $P_0P_6$, and $P_9P_{11}$ crosses only $P_4P_{10}$: exactly $3$.
3. Blue: $P_0P_2,\ P_4P_6,\ P_8P_{10}$. Red: $P_1P_5,\ P_3P_9,\ P_7P_{11}$. $P_1P_5$ crosses $P_0P_2$ and $P_4P_6$; $P_3P_9$ crosses $P_8P_{10}$ only; $P_7P_{11}$ crosses none: exactly $3$.

They are pairwise non-equivalent under rotation: in (1) and (2) each red chord crosses exactly one blue chord, but in (1) the blue chords are short (they join neighbouring blue points) while in (2) they are long (they join opposite points); in (3) the red chords cross $2,1,0$ blue chords. An exhaustive computer search finds $22$ rotation classes with $3$ good pairs.

prompt:
Fix a positive integer $n$. Pick $4n$ equally spaced points on a circle and color them alternately blue and red. You use $n$ blue chords to pair the $2n$ blue points, and you use $n$ red chords to pair the $2n$ red points. If some blue chord intersects some other red chord, then such a pair of chords is called a "good pair."

Find, with proof, the minimum number of good pairs under all possible configurations of chord pairings.

solutions.title: Uncross the red chords, then count parity
solutions.body:
**Answer: $n$.**

*Uncrossing lemma.* Suppose two red chords $AC$ and $BD$ cross, with $A,B,C,D$ in this cyclic order. Replace them by $AB$ and $CD$. The total length of the red chords strictly decreases (triangle inequality at the crossing point $X$: $AX+XB>AB$, $CX+XD>CD$), so since there are finitely many pairings, repeating the replacement terminates, and in the end no two red chords cross.

*The replacement never increases the number of good pairs.* Take a blue chord $EF$. If $E,F$ lie in the same one of the four arcs $AB,BC,CD,DA$, it crosses none of the four chords either before or after. If they lie in adjacent arcs it crosses exactly one of $\{AC,BD\}$ and exactly one of $\{AB,CD\}$. If they lie in the opposite arcs $AB$ and $CD$ it crosses two of each. If they lie in the opposite arcs $BC$ and $DA$ it crosses $AC$ and $BD$ but neither $AB$ nor $CD$. So the count never increases (it drops by $2$ in the last case).

*Lower bound.* Take a configuration with no two red chords crossing (after uncrossing; the number of good pairs is at most that of the original). Consider any red chord $XY$ and the arc on one side of it. The other red points on this arc are matched among themselves (no red chord crosses $XY$), so their number is even. Since colours alternate and $X,Y$ are red, that arc has one more blue point than red points, i.e. an odd number of blue points. The blue chords with both ends on the arc use an even number of them, so some blue chord has exactly one end on the arc, and it crosses $XY$. So each of the $n$ red chords is in at least one good pair, and different red chords give different pairs. Hence at least $n$ good pairs.

*Construction with $n$ good pairs.* Label the points $A_1,\dots,A_{4n}$ around the circle, odd indices blue and even indices red. Use the blue diameter $A_1A_{2n+1}$, the other blue chords $A_{2k+1}A_{4n+1-2k}$ ($1\le k\le n-1$), and the red chords $A_{2k}A_{4n+2-2k}$ ($1\le k\le n$). Every chord other than the diameter joins mirror-image points in the diameter, so is perpendicular to it, hence all these chords are parallel and do not cross each other. So the only crossings between a red and a blue chord are the $n$ crossings of the red chords with the blue diameter: exactly $n$ good pairs.

Therefore the minimum is $n$. ∎

prompt: Let $a,b,c$ be real numbers. Given that $a\cos x+b\cos2x+c\cos3x\ge-1$ for all reals $x$, find, with proof, the maximum possible value of $a+b+c$.

solutions.title: Evaluate at 0, pi/2, pi
solutions.body:
Let $h(x)=a\cos x+b\cos2x+c\cos3x\ge-1$. Then $h(0)=a+b+c$, $h\left(\frac\pi2\right)=-b$, $h(\pi)=-a+b-c$, so $h(0)+2h\left(\frac\pi2\right)+h(\pi)=0$ and
$$a+b+c=h(0)=-2h\left(\tfrac\pi2\right)-h(\pi)\le2+1=3.$$
Equality is attained: $a=\frac32,b=1,c=\frac12$ gives $h(x)=\frac32\cos x+(2\cos^2x-1)+\frac12(4\cos^3x-3\cos x)=2\cos^3x+2\cos^2x-1=2\cos^2x(\cos x+1)-1\ge-1$.

**Answer: 3**

prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer and $f$ a degree $n$ polynomial with real coefficients. Suppose that $|f(z)|\le\left|f(z)+\frac2z\right|$ for all complex $z$ lying on the unit circle. Find, with proof, the maximum possible value of $f(1)$.

solutions.title: Averaging over roots of unity
solutions.body:
**Answer: $n+1$.**

For $|z|=1$, $\left|f+\frac2z\right|^2-|f|^2=4\,\mathrm{Re}(zf(z))+4$ (since $\overline{1/z}=z$), so the condition is $\mathrm{Re}\big(zf(z)\big)\ge-1$. Write $f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^na_jx^j$ with real $a_j$ and $z=e^{i\theta}$: the condition becomes
$$h(\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^na_j\cos((j+1)\theta)\ge-1\quad\text{for all }\theta,$$
and $f(1)=\sum a_j=h(0)$.

*Upper bound.* Let $\theta_k=\frac{2\pi k}{n+2}$. For each $m=j+1\in\{1,\dots,n+1\}$, $\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}\cos(m\theta_k)=0$ (sum of the real parts of all $(n+2)$-th roots of unity raised to the power $m$, with $n+2\nmid m$). So $\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}h(\theta_k)=0$ and
$$f(1)=h(0)=-\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}h(\theta_k)\le(n+1)\cdot1=n+1.$$

*Attained.* Take $a_j=\frac{2(n+1-j)}{n+2}$. Then $\sum a_j=\frac2{n+2}\cdot\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}2=n+1$, and using $\sum_{j=1}^s\cos j\theta=\frac{\sin((s+\frac12)\theta)-\sin\frac\theta2}{2\sin\frac\theta2}$ one gets for $\theta\not\equiv0$
$$h(\theta)=\frac{2}{n+2}\sum_{s=1}^{n+1}\sum_{j=1}^s\cos j\theta=\frac{1-\cos((n+2)\theta)}{(n+2)\sin^2\frac\theta2}-1\ge-1,$$
and $h(0)=n+1\ge-1$. So the condition holds and $f(1)=n+1$. ∎

prompt:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcenter $O$. The interior bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects $BC$ at $D$. Circle $\omega_A$ is tangent to segments $AB$ and $AC$ and internally tangent to the circumcircle of $ABC$ at the point $P$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the respective points at which the $B$-excircle and $C$-excircle of $ABC$ are tangent to $AC$ and $AB$. Suppose that lines $BE$ and $CF$ pass through a common point $N$ on the circumcircle of $AEF$.

Prove that the circumcircle of $PDO$ passes through $N$.
answer: $N$ is the Nagel point; it lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, and $A,O,D,P,N$ are concyclic.

solutions.title: Nagel point and an inversion
solutions.body:
Notation: $H$ orthocentre, $G$ centroid, $I$ incentre, $A'B'C'$ the medial triangle, $M$ the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$, $K_2$ the point where the $A$-excircle touches $BC$.

*Step 1: $N$ is the Nagel point and lies on $(BHC)$.* Lines $BE,CF$ (and $AK_2$) concur at the Nagel point, so $N$ is the Nagel point. Since $N\in(AEF)$, $\angle ENF=180^\circ-\angle A=\angle BHC$, so $N\in(BHC)$.

*Step 2: $I$ is the Nagel point of the medial triangle $A'B'C'$.* The incircle and $A$-excircle are homothetic from $A$; if $Q$ is the antipode of the incircle's contact point $K_1$ on $BC$, then $A,Q,N,K_2$ are collinear. As $I$ and $A'$ are midpoints of $K_1Q$ and $K_1K_2$, $IA'\parallel AK_2=AN$. With $A'B'\parallel AB$ and $A'C'\parallel AC$ this shows that the cevian $A'I$ of the medial triangle corresponds to the cevian $AN$, likewise for $B$ and $C$, so $I$ is the Nagel point of $A'B'C'$.

*Step 3: $BN=CN$.* The homothety with centre $G$ and ratio $-\frac12$ maps $ABC\to A'B'C'$, $H\to O$ (Euler line) and $N\to I$. As $B',C',O$ are on the circle with diameter $AO$ (right angles at $B',C'$), $I$ is on it too; since $AI$ bisects $\angle B'AC'$, $I$ is the midpoint of arc $B'C'$, so $IB'=IC'$, and by the correspondence $NB=NC$. So $N$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ and on $(BHC)$: $N$ is the reflection in $BC$ of $M$ (the reflection of $(BHC)$ in $BC$ is $(ABC)$).

*Step 4: $A,P,D,O$ concyclic.* Let $\mathcal J$ be the inversion in the circle of centre $A$ and radius $\sqrt{AB\cdot AC}$ followed by reflection in $AD$. It is well known that $\mathcal J$ sends $M\mapsto D$, the reflection $A''$ of $A$ in $BC\mapsto O$, and the $A$-excircle to the mixtilinear incircle $\omega_A$, hence $K_2\mapsto P$. Reflecting $A,N,K_2$ in $BC$ gives $A'',M,K_2$, which are collinear. A line not through $A$ maps to a circle through $A$: so $A,O,D,P$ are concyclic.

*Step 5: $A,O,N,D$ concyclic.* Because $N,M$ are symmetric in $BC$ and $D\in BC$, $MD=ND$; and $MO=AO$. So triangles $AOM$ and $NDM$ are isosceles with the common angle at $M$ and are similar; hence $ND$ and $AO$ are antiparallel with respect to the angle at $M$, giving that $A,O,N,D$ are concyclic.

*Conclusion.* The circles $(AODP)$ and $(AODN)$ share the three points $A,O,D$, so they coincide and $N$ lies on the circle through $P,D,O$. ∎

reviewNote: Several steps (Nagel-point facts, the inversion J mapping M to D and the A-excircle to the mixtilinear incircle) are quoted from the official solution as well-known results rather than proved.

prompt: In the setting of the previous part (triangle $ABC$ with circumcentre $O$, interior bisector $AD$ with $D$ on $BC$, circle $\omega_A$ tangent to $AB,AC$ and internally tangent to the circumcircle at $P$, points $E,F$ the tangency points of the $B$- and $C$-excircles with $AC$ and $AB$, and lines $BE,CF$ meeting at a point $N$ on the circumcircle of $AEF$), suppose that $\frac{PD}{BC}=\frac27$. Find, with proof, the value of $\cos(\angle BAC)$.

solutions.title: From the previous part
solutions.body:
From the proof of the previous part: $I$ (the incentre) is the midpoint of $AM$, with $M$ the midpoint of arc $BC$, and $IM=MC$; so $AM=2MC$. Triangles $ABD$ and $AMC$ are similar ($\angle ABD=\angle AMC$, $\angle BAD=\angle MAC$) so $\frac{AC}{DC}=\frac{AB}{DB}=\frac{AM}{MC}=2$, whence $b+c=2a$ in the usual notation. Also $D$ is the midpoint of $IM$.

Since $A,P,D,N$ are concyclic and $\angle PAD=\angle DAN$ (the circle $\omega_A$ is symmetric about the bisector, so $AP$ and $AN$ are isogonal), the chords $PD$ and $DN$ are equal. Also $DN=DM$ ($N,M$ symmetric in $BC$) and $DM=\frac12IM$ ($D$ is the midpoint of $IM$) and $IM=AI$ ($I$ is the midpoint of $AM$). So $PD=\frac12AI$, and the hypothesis becomes $\frac{AI}{BC}=\frac47$.

Let $\alpha=\angle BAC$, $r,R$ the in- and circumradii. With $b+c=2a$ the tangent length from $A$ to the incircle is $s-a=\frac a2$ (as $s=\frac{3a}2$), and also $s-a=\frac r{\tan(\alpha/2)}$, so $a=\frac{2r}{\tan(\alpha/2)}$; by the law of sines $a=2R\sin\alpha$, so $r=R(1-\cos\alpha)$. Then
$$\frac{AI}{BC}=\frac{r/\sin\frac\alpha2}{2R\sin\alpha}=\frac{1-\cos\alpha}{2\sin\alpha\sin\frac\alpha2}=\frac{\tan\frac\alpha2}{2\sin\frac\alpha2}=\frac1{2\cos\frac\alpha2}=\frac47.$$
So $\cos\frac\alpha2=\frac78$ and $\cos\alpha=2\cdot\frac{49}{64}-1=\frac{17}{32}$. (A direct numerical construction with $a=2,b=\frac{16}7,c=\frac{12}7$, which has $b+c=2a$ and $\cos\alpha=\frac{17}{32}$, confirms $N\in(AEF)$ and $\frac{PD}{BC}=\frac27$.)

**Answer: $\frac{17}{32}$**
